clinical.vignette: This is a 35-year-old female with clinically suspected appendicitis. Diagnosis?

answer.text:
Histologic Description:

In this resection, we see a portion of appendix with submucosal adipose tissue, fibrous tissue, and benign appearing glands scattered throughout the muscularis propria. There are a number of vessels with hypertrophic smooth muscle. At high power, there are endometrioid glands with scant areas of endometrial type stroma, consistent with Mullerian-osis/endometriosis.

IHC: (+) CD10 (stroma), PAX8, ER

Differential diagnosis:

fibrous obliteration of the appendix, invasive adenocarcinoma (negative: ER)

Reference:

clinical.vignette: This is a 25-year-old male with pancreas cysts. Diagnosis?

answer.text:
Histologic Description:

Here, we see a portion of pancreas with dilated cystic spaces, lined by epithelium. At higher power, we see the epithelium is comprised of cuboidal cells with acinar like nuclei and chromatin pattern and without atypia or mitoses. Notably, no ovarian type stroma is seen in the adjacent stromal tissue. This is consistent with an acinar cell cystadenoma of the pancreas (acinar cystic transformation).

IHC: (+) BCL10, CK19, trypsin, PAS

Differential diagnosis:

serous cystadenoma (positive: PAS negative: PAS-D), retention cyst, simple mucinous cyst

clinical.vignette: This is an adult with a lung wedge resection. Diagnosis?

answer.text:
Histologic Description:

Here, we see a portion of lung with well circumscribed mass, an adenoid cystic carcinoma. At higher power, we see this epithelioid neoplasm with glandular, papillary, pseudo/cystic areas involving large vessels, septa, and peripherally lining alveolar spaces. These hyperchromatic cells feature minimal cytoplasm, seem to be hobnailing into alveolar spaces, and feature coarse chromatin, with prominent nucleoli.

IHC: (+) CK7, P63, SMA, S100 (myoepithelial component), keratin (epithelial component), CD117

Molecular: t(6;9)(MYB-NFIB)

Differential diagnosis:

adenocarcinoma (positive: TTF1, NapsinA negative: S100, CD117), epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma (no cribriform structures), small cell carcinoma (negative: MYB-NFIB fusion)

answer.text:
Histologic Description:

At low power, the slide features a portion of cardiac muscle, hemosiderin and hemorrhage with a large, well circumscribed mass. clinical.vignette: This is a 41 year old male with renal mass.

choices: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumor

answer.text:
Histologic Description:

This is a case that demonstrates striking hyalinization within the primary tumor, leading to negative scans performed in radiology. Away from the extensive hyalinization, one can appreciate areas of nested to papillary architecture and neoplastic epithelioid cells with abundant pale to eosinophilic cytoplasm. These cells label diffusely for TFE3 and demonstrate rearrangement of TFE3 by FISH.

Differential Diagnosis:

Clear cell renal cell carcinoma could demonstrate hyalinization like this, but would be expected to label for carbonic anhydrase 9 and not for TFE3. Papillary renal cell carcinoma may have clear cell areas in regions of hemorrhage. It would not demonstrate the extensive hyalinization seen in the current case. Clear cell papillary renal cell tumor is typically not extensively hyalinized, and should feature low grade nuclei. It would label for cytokeratin 7 and carbonic anhydrase 9, not for TFE3. Xp11 translocation RCC and TFEB rearranged RCC often demonstrate striking stromal hyalinization, likely reflecting their slow proliferative rates and gradual fibrosis.

differential: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumor

clinical.vignette: This is a 40 year old female with a history of pneumothorax and pleural biopsy. Diagnosis?

answer.text:
Histologic Description:

The pleura contains areas of striking chronic inflammation with hemosiderin deposition and paucicellular fibrosis. Focally between the inflammatory cells are more cellular areas consisting of bland spindle cells associated with prominent capillary vasculature. The spindle cells label diffusely for estrogen receptor and for CD10, consistent with endometrial stroma This patient had a history of endometriosis in other organ sites.

Differential Diagnosis:

Organizing hematoma could have similar features, though the cellular spindle cell proliferation would not be typical. Organizing hematoma would not be expected to label diffusely for estrogen receptor. Spindle cell mesothelioma would demonstrate greater nuclear atypia and would label for cytokeratin. Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma typically features more epithelioid neoplastic cells in myxochondroid matrix. It would not be expected to label for estrogen receptor.

Endometriosis involving the pleura can present as recurrent pneumothorax.

clinical.vignette: This is a 60 year old male with long standing ulcerative colitis. Diagnosis?

answer.text:
P53 Immunohistochemistry:

Histologic Description:

There is a prominent giant cell reaction in the bowel wall consistent with prior endoscopic mucosal resection. The colon demonstrates the typical features of ulcerative colitis, including increased chronic inflammation with basal cell plasmacytosis and crypt distortion, along with activity in the form of cryptitis. The lesional crypts demonstrate minimally-stratified nuclei generally limited to the crypt base with mild nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia and irregularity. They do stand out from the surrounding reactive epithelial changes. By immunohistochemistry, these areas diffusely overexpress p53 protein.

Differential Diagnosis:

Hypermucinous dysplasia would demonstrate lower N/C ratio and prominent cytoplasmic and luminal mucin. Reactive changes would not demonstrate the nuclear irregularity of the current lesion and diffuse p53 labeling. Conventional dysplasia typically involves the surface epithelium, and demonstrates greater degrees of nuclear stratification and irregularity.

There is limited outcome data on the behavior of crypt cell dysplasia, but there is reason to consider it high grade based upon cases that have progressed.

Reference:

Histopathology 2021; 78:658-675.

clinical.vignette: Clinical History: A 68 year-old man underwent a prostatic needle biopsy for elevated serum PSA. Choose the correct diagnosis:

choices: Stromal tumor of uncertain malignant potential (STUMP)

answer.diagnosis: Stromal tumor of uncertain malignant potential (STUMP)
answer.text:
Histologic description:

The lesion consists of slightly hypercellular stroma with scattered atypical, but degenerative appearing cells. The adjacent glands are crowded with basal cell hyperplasia. The lesion lacks mitotic figures and in particular atypical mitotic figures.

Discussion:

This is the most common pattern of STUMP. Other patterns include: 1) hypercellular stroma consisting of bland fusiform stromal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm admixed with benign glands; 2) myxoid stroma containing bland stromal cells and often lacking admixed glands in sheets of stroma without nodularity, lacking the thick walled vessels of BPH; 3) phyllodes with leaf-like hypocellular fibrous stroma covered by benign appearing prostatic epithelium; and 4) round cell with increased stromal cellularity composed of cells with round bland nuclei, in contrast to stromal BPH nuclei which are oval and spindled. STUMPS may recur within a few months or years after TURP only. STUMPs have been associated with stromal sarcoma on concurrent biopsy material or have demonstrated stromal sarcoma on repeat biopsy, suggesting a malignant progression in at least some cases. If a STUMP is entirely resected and there is no sarcomatous component, then the lesion is entirely cured. Some cases of prostatic stromal sarcoma can resemble a STUMP, but will be more cellular and often have increased mitotic figures including atypical ones. Immunohistochemistry is not helpful in the differential diagnosis as STUMP, stromal sarcoma, and stromal BPH will be positive for CD34, smooth muscle actin, desmin, and progesterone receptor. If sarcomatoid carcinoma was being considered, high molecular weight cytokeratin and p63 would be helpful, as the glands would contain basal cells. Although the primary process in a STUMP is stromal, they are often accompanied by glandular proliferations, such as basal cell hyperplasia, adenosis, cribriform hyperplasia, squamous and urothelial metaplasia.

clinical.vignette: Clinical History: A 48-year-old man underwent a transurethral resection of the prostate. Choose the correct diagnosis:

choices: Stromal tumor of uncertain malignant potential (STUMP) with necrosis
Low grade prostatic stromal sarcoma with necrosis

answer.text:
Histologic description:

The TUR is completely composed of moderately hypercellular stroma. In some areas, nodularity can be appreciated. Scattered throughout the stroma are thick-walled capillaries. Areas of the stroma are necrotic.

Discussion:

The most common stromal lesion sent to me in consultation is stromal nodular BPH. The key to recognizing cellular stromal BPH are small capillaries that in cross-section have relatively thick walls for the size of the vessels. In settings other than BPH, these small vessels would not be expected to have such thick walls and typically no apparent wall at all. The unusual aspect to this case is the necrosis. Prominent BPH can undergo infarction, but typically it is with glandular-stromal nodular BPH, where the histological pitfall is reactive urothelial metaplasia mimicking urothelial carcinoma in the prostate glands immediately adjacent to the necrotic center of the infarct. In the current case, it is a purely stromal BPH that has undergone infarction. In addition to the classic capillaries of BPH that are not seen in STUMPs or prostatic stromal sarcomas, the lesion lacks the atypia that would be seen in a stromal sarcoma of the prostate.

differential: Stromal tumor of uncertain malignant potential (STUMP) with necrosis
Low grade prostatic stromal sarcoma with necrosis

answer.text:
Histologic description:

The lesion consists of several simple folds of normal thickness urothelium with some that appear as detached papillary fronds and others that are edemetous. Within the urothelium are scattered neutrophils. The lamina propria is fibrotic with chronic inflammation.

Discussion:

The clinicopathological findings in this case is classic for polypoid cystitis. The key to not misdiagnosis polypoid cystitis as a papillary urothelial neoplasm is to look at the overall low power histological appearance, as opposed to focusing on the few papillary fronds that out of context could be mistaken for a papilloma or PUNLMP. Overall the presence of predominantly simple folds lined by normal thickness and cytology inflamed urothelium is classic for polypoid cystitis. This case has less edema in the lamina propria and more fibrosis, indicative of a more chronic phase of polypoid cystitis. Some cases of polypoid cystitis can have numerous mitotic figures in the urothelium and have reactive urothelial changes with prominent nucleoli and enlarge nuclei, but lacking hyperchromasia. In cases where the diagnosis is not straightforward histologically, it is helpful to review the cystoscopic findings as they are typically that of an inflammatory process, such as a reaction to a calculus, colo-vesicle fistula, catheter, or even long-standing urinary obstruction. The urologist can often more readily appreciate the inflammatory nature of the process better than the pathologist.

clinical.vignette: This is an orchiectomy specimen from a 51-year-old man. Diagnosis?

answer.text:
Sections show a bland cystic lesion lined by low grade intestinal type epithelium. The patient’s age as well as the calcifications, scar, and Sertoli-only seen in the background testis strongly argue against a pre-pubertal type teratoma, as the vast majority of testicular teratomas in adults are malignant. As epidermoid cyst is essentially a monodermal benign teratoma composed of a unilocular cyst lined by bland squamous epithelium, that diagnosis may also be excluded based on the cyst lining and abnormal background testis. The patient clinically presented with distant metastasis, also excluding a benign teratoma. The lack of a colonic primary excludes metastasis to the testis. The combined findings are diagnostic of a malignant, post-pubertal teratoma and the adjacent scarring is indicative of regression, likely explaining why the patient presented with metastatic disease rather than a testicular mass.

clinical.vignette: This specimen is from the bladder of a 56-year-old man. Diagnosis?

answer.text:
Sections show a high-grade malignant tumor composed of small round blue cells. Immunohistochemistry will be required to determine the lineage. Lack of desmin or myogenin labeling excludes rhabdomyosarcoma, which may label with keratin and or neuroendocrine markers, so warrants exclusion before diagnosing neuroendocrine carcinoma. Diffuse large B cell lymphoma would lack keratin expression and will label with CD20 and other B-cell markers. Prostatic adenocarcinoma would label with NKX3.1. This tumor labeled with cytokeratin, synaptophysin and TTF1, indicative of small cell carcinoma. The lack of concurrent or previous prostatic adenocarcinoma were most in keeping with a bladder primary, although based on morphology alone it is difficult to exclude a prostatic primary.

clinical.vignette: This specimen is from an 88-year-old male with a skin lesion. Diagnosis?

answer.text:
Sections show a malignant-appearing pleomorphic tumor involving dermis. An associated epithelial component or convincing keratin or P40 expression would be diagnostic of sarcomatoid squamous carcinoma. Expression of melanocytic markers would support melanoma. The presence of numerous mitotic figures, including atypical forms and the lack of CD34 expression exclude superficial CD34+ fibroblastic tumor, although this lesion also may be at risk for overdiagnosis as pleomorphic sarcoma. The morphologically malignant undifferentiated appearance, null immunophenotype, lack of perineural or lymphatic invasion and lack of subcutis involvement are the diagnostic features of atypical fibroxanthoma, which despite an overtly malignant morphology, has a benign clinical course. If perineural or lymphatic invasion or subcutis involvement were present, then a diagnosis of pleomorphic dermal sarcoma, which has a risk of recurrence and/or metastasis, would be warranted.

Reference:

Polcz MM, Sebaratnam DF, Fernández-Peñas P. Atypical fibroxanthoma management: Recurrence, metastasis and disease-specific death. Australas J Dermatol. 2018 Feb;59(1):10-25. doi: 10.1111/ajd.12646. Epub 2017 Aug 17. PMID: 28815551.

clinical.vignette: This specimen is from a 50-year-old male with thyroid nodules. Diagnosis?

answer.text:
Sections show discohesive clear and epithelioid cells arranged in nodules breaking through follicles (distinguishing from C-cell hyperplasia) and surrounding areas with prominent stromal response and amyloid deposition. These cells have “salt and pepper” chromatin. Patients with MEN2a and MEN2b syndromes are at an increased risk for developing these tumors. These tumors often contain activating mutations in the RET tyrosine kinase. Due to the origin of these tumors from the ultimobranchial body during development, these tumors arise in the upper half of the thyroid lobes and do not occur in the isthmus. Immunohistochemistry for neuroendocrine markers (synaptophysin, chromogranin, INSM1) is positive, as well as calcitonin (vs paraganglioma and parathyroid adenoma), TTF-1 and PAX8.

answer.text:
Sections show a well circumscribed basophilic mass of epithelioid cells and lymphocytes. clinical.vignette: This is a kidney biopsy of a 47-year-old female. Diagnosis?

answer.text:
Sections show a bland spindle cell neoplasm with keloidal collagen and vaguely nested to fascicular growth. Leiomyoma is vanishingly rare in the kidney and would have more overt fascicular growth with dense eosinophilic cytoplasm, and typically lacks expression of melanocytic markers. Translocation RCC may label with melanocytic markers and/or cathepsin-K but typically expresses PAX8 and/or cytokeratin. Sarcomatoid renal cell carcinoma will be overtly malignant histologically and expression of keratin and/or PAX8 would support the diagnosis. Angiomyolipoma is the most common benign spindle cell neoplasm in the kidney and may lack a fatty component, leading to concern for renal cell carcinoma radiographically. Labeling with cathepsin-K supports the diagnosis, as does the subtly vacuolated pink cytoplasm with intracytoplasmic filaments, a feature that is suggestive of the diagnosis of PEComa at both renal as well as extra-renal sites.

Reference:

Lane BR, Aydin H, Danforth TL, Zhou M, Remer EM, Novick AC, Campbell SC. Clinical correlates of renal angiomyolipoma subtypes in 209 patients: classic, fat poor, tuberous sclerosis associated and epithelioid. clinical.vignette: This is a nephrectomy specimen from a 68-year-old male. Diagnosis?

choices: Multilocular cystic renal neoplasm of low malignant potential
Fumarate hydratase deficient renal cell carcinoma

answer.text:
Sections show a high-grade multicystic neoplasm composed entirely of cysts of variable size lined by hobnail epithelium with eosinophilic cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli, and irregular nuclear contours. Fumarate hydratase deficient renal cell carcinoma can have similar cytology and can have multicystic areas but often also displays areas of solid or papillary architecture and infiltrative growth. Retained FH staining and lack of 2SC expression argue against that diagnosis. Oncocytoma can have areas with tubular and/or cystic growth but the nuclei should lack irregularity and at least focally the architecture should consist of rounded nests within edematous/fibromyxoid stroma. Diffuse CK7 expression would exclude oncocytoma. Multilocular cystic renal neoplasm of low malignant potential is exclusively cystic but the lining cells have optically clear cytoplasm and the nests of clear cells should be confined to the septae of the cysts without deforming them with expansile nodules.

answer.text:
Sections show a malignant spindle cell tumor with extensive necrosis based in the renal pelvis. An associated epithelial component either invasive or in-situ would be diagnostic of sarcomatoid carcinoma, either renal cell or urothelial. In the absence of an epithelial component, immunohistochemistry to provide evidence of epithelial differentiation and lineage can be helpful. This tumor also labeled with keratin and GATA3 while negative for PAX8, supporting sarcomatoid urothelial carcinoma. Melanoma would be expected to express SOX10. Although mesothelioma could certainly express cytokeratin and GATA3, the history of urothelial carcinoma, epicenter of the tumor in the renal pelvis and lack of peritoneal disease, and lack of expression of other mesothelial markers exclude that diagnosis.

clinical.vignette: This case is a testicular mass arising in an adult male.

answer.text:
Answer: C. Teratoma with somatic-type malignancy

Histology: This lesion is a teratoma consisting of a heterogenous solid and cystic mass with neural, epithelial, muscular, and connective tissue elements. Rhabdomyoblasts with eosinophilic cytoplasm are infiltrating throughout the tissue with large, poorly defined nodular areas containing rhabdomyoblasts with atypical morphology and areas of small round blue cells consisting of a primitive component.

Discussion: This lesion is a rhabdomyosarcoma arising from a testicular teratoma. Multiple types of malignant transformation are possible within a teratoma, with the most common being sarcomas, primitive neuroectodermal tumors, and carcinomas. The prognosis of a somatic malignancy within a teratoma is dependent on the stage of the lesion at diagnosis, with complete surgical excision recommended if possible. In general, somatic malignancies arising within a teratoma are less responsive to systemic therapy. There is not a generalizable prognostic implication for the subtype of somatic malignancies. The diagnostic criterion for a secondary malignancy within a teratoma is defined in the WHO as an area measuring 5mm in diameter in which only one element is exclusively found. Cytologic atypia cannot be the lone determinant of malignancy.

answer.text:
Answer: D. Metanephric adenoma

Histology: This lesion is a well circumscribed, non-encapsulated mass consisting of bland epithelioid cells with scant cytoplasm forming small tubules and trabecular-shaped structures. The cells are relatively uniform appearing with a very low mitotic activity and no invasion into surrounding structures.

Discussion: Metanephric adenoma is a rare, benign neoplastic renal lesion typically presenting as a well circumscribed mass in older adults. The tumor is cellular and can have psammoma bodies as well as scant areas of scarred stroma. A large majority of these tumors are reported to have a BRAF mutation, specifically a V600E mutation. Immunostains will typically be positive for PAX-8, WT-1, and CD57. The tumor can have patchy to negative CK7, unlike papillary renal cell carcinoma which is CK7 positive and WT-1 negative, and will stain negative for CD56, unlike a nephroblastoma which is CD56 positive and CD57 negative.

answer.text:
Answer: B. Fibrothecoma

Histology: This lesion is a well circumscribed mass consisting of bland appearing spindled to epithelioid cells with scattered large calcifications. The lesion displays areas of alternating hyper- and hypocellularity heterogeneously distributed across the mass, with areas of higher cellularity having a collagenous stroma. This tumor has low mitotic activity and does not invade adjacent seminiferous tubules.

Discussion: Fibrothecomas are a rare subset of sex cord stromal tumors occurring in the testis with the histologic features described above. These tumors usually arise in connection to the tunica albuginea and grow inwards into the testicular parenchyma, outwards into the tunica vaginalis or both. The most common clinical presentation is as a painless testicular mass. The treatment is complete excision, most commonly as an orchiectomy, and have a benign clinical course. Immunostains for inhibin, SF1, calretinin, ER/PR are positive, while HMB-45 and CD34 are negative.

clinical.vignette: A 35 year-old man underwent an orchiectomy for a 1.5 cm. testicular mass.

answer.text:
Answer: D

Histologic description: The tumor is relatively well-circumscribed, although not encapsulated, and abuts the tunica albuginea. Focal extension into the surrounding testis is noted with entrapment of seminiferous tubules. The tumor is composed of cellular short fascicles and a storiform pattern. Cells range from having plumper ovoid as opposed to spindled pointed nuclei, lacking prominent nucleoli. Collagen deposition is scant. Mitotic figures are present, but not frequent.

Discussion: Fibrothecoma a sex cord stromal tumor of the testis that is analogous to those more commonly seen in the ovary. The mean age at diagnosis is 44 years (16 to 69 y). The median size is 2 cm, yet can range up to 7.6 cm. Cases are always intratesticular, with most abutting the tunica albuginea as in the current case. Other are centered on the rete testis. Although most cases have had 0 to 2 mitoses per 10 HPF, they may have up to 9 to 10 mitoses per 10 HPF. Collagen deposition either in bands or investing single cells can range from none to extensive, with most having at least a moderate amount. Immunohistochemically, the most sensitive and specific stain is Steroid Factor 1 (SF-1). Other positivity that is not as specific or sensitive is with inhibin, calretinin, Melan-A, pan keratin, CD34, S100 protein, muscle-specific actin, and desmin. Amongst the lesions listed in the differential diagnosis, monophasic synovial sarcoma is the closest mimicker of fibrothecoma. Synovial sarcomas do not occur in the testis and would be negative for SF-1. It is important to recognize testicular fibrothecomas, as despite in some cases hypercellularity, larger size, and frequent mitotic figures, they are totally benign.

clinical.vignette: A 48 year-old man underwent a transurethral resection of a bladder mass.

choices: Non-invasive low grade papillary urothelial carcinoma with inverted pattern
Papillary urothelial neoplasm of low malignant potential (PUNLMP) with inverted pattern
Florid proliferation of von Brunn nests

answer.text:
Answer: C

Histologic description: At low magnification, the surface is smooth with only rare exophytic papillary fronds. In some areas, there is continuity of the lesion with the surface but in most area this feature is lacking. The lamina propria is filled with anastomosing thin columns of urothelium. In areas the periphery of columns are lined by cells with a palisading appearance, where cells stream parallel to the basement membrane in the center of nests. Focal small cysts with colloid material is identified. There is no cytological atypia with some cells with nuclear grooves. Mitotic figures are rare and when present only at the periphery of columns. There are small cyst formations filled with eosinophilic secretions. The intervening stroma is delicate with lack of inflammation.

Discussion: Inverted papillomas occurs any location in the urothelial tract, yet most common in the trigone or bladder neck. At cystoscopy, the lesion appears polypoid with a smooth surface. Tumors are almost always unifocal. They are usually < 3 cm., but have a wide range in size. It is rare for PUNLMPs or non-invasive low grade papillary urothelial carcinoma to have a purely or almost purely inverted growth pattern without a more prominent exophytic papillary frond component. In the setting of an almost exclusively inverted tumor, one should always consider inverted papilloma. Inverted papillomas also lack any cytological atypia in contrast to low grade papillary urothelial carcinoma. In addition, inverted papillomas are composed of anastomosing columns as opposed to large rounded nests when there is inverted growth in PUNLMP or low grade papillary urothelial carcinoma. In contrast to urothelial carcinoma, inverted papillomas have no risk of recurrence or progression to urothelial carcinoma.

clinical.vignette: A 55 year-old woman underwent a resection of a 3.0 cm. renal mass.

choices: Eosinophilic solid and cystic renal cell carcinoma (ESC RCC)

answer.text:
Answer: A

Histologic description: The tumor is circumscribed but unencapsulated. The lesion is composed of nests with focal tubular architecture. Cytologically, there are uniform cells with voluminous oncocytic cytoplasm and frequent prominent clear intracytoplasmic vacuoles. Nuclei are round to oval, often irregular with prominent nucleoli.

Discussion: Eosinophilic and vacuolated tumor (EVT) is a newly recognized renal tumor. It has also been reported as “high-grade oncocytic tumor (HOT)” or “sporadic RCC with eosinophilic and vacuolated cytoplasm”. It is seen a unifocal tumor, mostly in females with a broad age range. The great majority of the tumors are sporadic, but rare tumors with identical morphology have been reported in patients with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC). Somatic and bi-allelic mutations in the TSC genes, TSC1 and TSC2 are present in these tumors. The presence of prominent vacuoles is virtually pathognomonic of this entity. In contrast, eosinophilic solid and cystic renal cell carcinoma (ESC RCC) lacks vacuoles, is often more cystic with hobnail cells, has clumped amphophilic cytoplasmic inclusions, and typically expresses CK20. HOT lacks CK20, CK7, and is positive for CD117. SDHB deficient RCC can have a similar architectural pattern and vacuoles. However, most SDHB deficient RCCs lack prominent nucleoli and the vacuoles are much smaller with pale eosinophilic or bubbly appearance and would show loss of SDHB immunohistochemically. To date, there have been no reports of metastases with EVTs, leading them to be designated as “tumors” as opposed to “carcinomas”.

clinical.vignette: This is an 80 year old female with multiple polyps in the fundus of her stomach.

answer.text:
Answer: C

Histologic Description: The polypoid lesions have features of gastric hyperplastic polyp. Within the polyps are areas of small blue cells which have solid and trabecular architecture, do not demonstrate areas of glandular architecture, and demonstrate fine dispersed chromatin. While there is minimal cytoplasm, the mitotic rate is low. The neoplastic cells label for chromogranin and synaptophysin, and the Ki67 is less than 2%. Further history reveals that this patient has a history of pernicious anemia. Areas of fundus (defined by absence of gastrin positive cells) demonstrate loss of parietal and chief cells, supporting the diagnosis of autoimmune metaplastic gastritis.

Discussion: The findings are consistent with type I gastric carcinoids arising in a background of autoimmune metaplastic atrophic gastritis. Differential Diagnosis: Poorly differentiated carcinoma would be a concern given the blue cell appearance of the lesion; however, the minimal mitotic activity argues against this possibility. The same argument can be made against small cell carcinoma in this case despite the immunoreactivity for neuroendocrine markers. Lymphoma is a concern given the high nucleus/cytoplasm ratio of the cells; however, the immunoreactivity for cytokeratin and neuroendocrine markers argues against this possibility.

The current tumors are examples of type I gastric carcinoids, which typically arise in autoimmune metaplastic atrophic gastritis, and are gastrin dependent lesions of the body and fundus associated with ECL cell hyperplasia. Type II gastric carcinoids are associated with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and are similarly located in the body and fundus. They are also associated with high gastrin levels from a neuroendocrine tumor elsewhere and ECL cell hyperplasia. Type III gastric carcinoids are sporadic, occur anywhere throughout the stomach, are solitary, and typically more aggressive.

choices: Clear cell papillary renal cell carcinoma

answer.text:
Answer: A

Histologic Description: The lesion has clear to eosinophilic cells, and both nested and papillary/pseudopapillary architectures. The vasculature of the lesion is prominent, with abundant proliferating endothelial cells. The areas of pseudopapillary growth are associated with higher nucleolar grade and eosinophilic cytoplasm. The lesional cells demonstrate diffuse membranous labeling for carbonic anhydrase 9 (CA-IX), and are negative for cytokeratin 7 and cathepsin K. They also demonstrate loss of BAP1, which correlates with high grade in clear cell RCC.

Differential Diagnosis: Xp11 translocation RCC does not demonstrate diffuse labeling for carbonic anhydrase 9; instead, the labeling is typically patchy if at all, and occurs in areas of necrosis. Papillary renal cell carcinoma also should not label diffusely for carbonic anhydrase 9, and typically labels diffusely for cytokeratin 7. Clear cell papillary renal cell carcinoma would demonstrate lower nuclear grade and features subnuclear vacuoles.

Clear cell RCC with a pseudopapillary growth pattern is a common mimic of Xp11 translocation renal cell carcinoma.

answer.text:
Answer: D. Malignant phyllodes tumor

Histology: This case depicts a fibroepithelial lesion that displays focal leaf-like architecture, marked stromal cellularity with moderate cytologic atypia, and a brisk mitotic rate (32 mitoses per 10 high power fields) including scattered atypical mitotic figures. The tumor displays an intracanalicular growth pattern, compressing the epithelium of the ducts it surrounds. Stromal overgrowth is present. These features are suggestive of a malignant phyllodes tumor.

Discussion: Fibroepithelial lesions of the breast consist of fibroadenomas and phyllodes tumors. Fibroadenomas are more common (>95% of fibroepithelial lesions) and are entirely benign. Phyllodes tumors are fibroepithelial lesions of the breast that display stromal hypercellularity and a prominent leaf-like architecture, often with cystic areas. In fact, their original name was “cystosarcoma phyllodes,” referring to the gross appearance: cystic (“cysto-“) and fleshy (“-sarcoma”), with projections resembling leaf fronds. The term “phyllodes” comes from the Greek “phyllon”, or leaf. Phyllodes tumors are subclassified into benign, borderline, and malignant based on their histologic features. When evaluating a fibroepithelial lesion, it’s helpful to first scan all slides of the lesions at low power to get an overall sense of the lesion, and then to evaluate these histologic features from low power to high power. In general, the severity of the atypia increases across the diagnostic categories of benign, borderline and malignant. The histologic features influencing classification include the degree of circumscription and infiltrative growth, stromal cellularity, stromal overgrowth (one 4x low power field entirely composed of stroma), stromal atypia, the mitotic rate, and the presence of malignant heterologous elements. The latter feature is present only in malignant phyllodes tumors. The histologic features in this case support classification as a malignant phyllodes tumor.

Answer: B. Cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis

Histology: This case depicts breast tissue with mixed acute, chronic, and granulomatous inflammation surrounding lobules and spanning larger portions of the breast biopsy cores. There are variably sized cystic spaces within the granulomatous inflammation. On high power inspection, the cystic spaces are rimmed with neutrophils.

Discussion: Cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis (CNGM) is a rare subtype of mastitis that is often associated with Corynebacterium infection, though this can be challenging to prove histologically. CNGM consists of granulomas or lipogranulomas with mixed inflammation, often centered around lobules within the breast. Lesions are typically unilateral and the majority present as a mass. Corynebacterium are gram positive bacilli and can be visible on gram stain (e.g., Gram-Weigert) within the cystic spaces. While cystic spaces are characteristic, and they are not strictly necessary for diagnosis. When granulomatous inflammation is present in the breast, mycobacterial or fungal infections should be considered. It is also important to rule out breast carcinomas, especially in older patients, as they can rarely have a granulomatous inflammatory reaction. If the patient has had previous surgical procedure in the breast, granulomatous inflammation can also result from a foreign body giant cell reaction to foreign materials.

answer.text:
Answer: B. Granular cell tumor

Histology: Examination of the breast tissue reveals an infiltrative lesion comprised of epithelioid cells with round nuclei, centrally located and prominent nucleoli, and abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm. The cells are infiltrating around and through benign ducts and lobules with no evidence of an atypical intraductal proliferation. There is minimal appreciable mitotic activity. Though not shown in this case, immunostains would show the cells to be diffusely immunoreactive for S100 and inhibin, and to be negative for AE1/AE3 and Cam5.2.

Discussion: This case depicts a granular cell tumor, which is a rare type of peripheral nerve sheath tumor arising from Schwann cells that can infrequently involve the breast. Granular cell tumors characteristically involve the head and neck and skin, where they can incite a prominent pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia in overlying squamous epithelium. In the breast, granular cell tumors clinically, radiographically and grossly mimic infiltrating carcinoma because they can appear as a fixed, stellate, and infiltrative solid mass. They may occur sporadically or in the setting of prior surgery. Histologically, granular cell tumors display abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm and can be either epithelioid or spindled, and occur either as nests of cells or as single-file rows of cells. The case illustrated here does exhibit atypical features including prominent nucleoli, but does not meet criteria for malignancy. The differential diagnosis includes histiocytic proliferations such as xanthogranulomatous inflammation and fat necrosis, as well as other pink cell tumors—melanoma, apocrine carcinomas, and histiocytoid lobular carcinomas. Immunohistochemistry can resolve any diagnostic dilemma, as granular cell tumors are immunoreactive for inhibin, CD68, S100 protein, and NSE, and are negative for cytokeratin and more specific melanocytic markers (HMB45, Melan A). Most granular cell tumors are benign and are adequately treated with complete surgical excision.

answer.text: Sections show skin with an intraepithelial population of neoplastic cells with ample cytoplasm with focal duct or gland formation. Melanoma in-situ could be considered, but in areas the tumor cells form clusters and glands with intracytoplasmic mucin, indicating glandular differentiation. Lack of SOX10 or Melan-A expression also excludes melanoma. Squamous cell carcinoma in-situ could show pagetoid growth, but tumor cells should label with squamous markers such as high molecular weight keratin and/or P63/40. A population of cytologically malignant glandular epithelial cells colonizing benign squamous epithelium is diagnostic of Paget’s disease. These cells often have an adnexal immunophenotype and can have an immunoprofile quite similar to breast carcinoma, including labeling with GATA3, GCDFP15, and/or mammaglobin in addition to ER/PR and/or HER2. On the basis of morphology alone, it is very difficult to distinguish from extension from an underlying visceral primary such as colon or bladder, therefore clinical evaluation for an underlying invasive or in-situ neoplasm is mandatory.

answer.diagnosis: Prostate adenocarcinoma, Grade Group 5, with pleomorphic giant cell features
answer.text: Sections show a high-grade cellular neoplasm with prominent nucleoli and papillary architecture. Paraganglioma can have abundant vascularity and marked nuclear atypia, but would typically show architecture that is more nested than papillary. Paragangliomas should lack keratin expression and would show labeling for neuroendocrine markers such as synaptophysin. Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma should have a high proliferation rate, often with basaloid nests with peripheral palisading. In the GU tract, this lesion should, by definition, lack any significant expression of prostate markers such as NKX3.1, PSA, or p501s, and should have significant expression of neuroendocrine markers. High grade papillary urothelial carcinoma can be difficult to distinguish from high grade prostatic adenocarcinoma invading the bladder, as both can show substantial papillary architecture. Marked nuclear pleomorphism, squamous differentiation, and an unequivocal precursor in-situ or non-invasive papillary urothelial neoplasm favor urothelial carcinoma. However, a low threshold for immunohistochemical confirmation is prudent given the substantial morphologic overlap. NKX3.1, p501s, and PSA expression indicate prostatic adenocarcinoma, whereas GATA3, uroplakin, and P63 are frequently expressed in urothelial carcinoma. Rare variants of prostatic adenocarcinoma in particular can mimic urothelial carcinoma. Adenosquamous carcinoma of the prostate can show bona fide squamous differentiation, and prostatic adenocarcinoma with pleomorphic giant cell features can show marked nuclear anaplasia, both leading to potential confusion with urothelial carcinoma. This patient had known recurrent prostatic adenocarcinoma causing urinary obstruction and bladder invasion. Despite the marked nuclear atypia and extensive papillary architecture, this tumor labeled diffusely with NKX3.1, confirming the diagnosis of prostatic adenocarcinoma with pleomorphic giant cell features.

answer.text: Sections show benign mesothelial lined fibrous tissue consistent with a hydrocele sac. Scattered cellular clusters of crushed small round blue cells are also seen. The cellularity of these clusters raises concern for a neoplasm, as in a different context such as a transbronchial lung biopsy these foci would be concerning for a neuroendocrine neoplasm. Answer: D. Chondro-osseous respiratory epithelial (CORE) hamartoma

Histology: The lesion consists of a disorganized proliferation of normal elements predominantly composed of ciliated respiratory epithelium with scattered intermixed seromucinous glands. The stroma is variably edematous with scattered chronic inflammation and central areas of bone. All components of the lesion are cytologically benign.

Discussion: The three most common sinonasal hamartomas are respiratory epithelial adenomatoid hamartoma (REAH), seromucinous hamartoma, and chondro-osseous respiratory epithelial (CORE) hamartoma. These hamartomas exist on a spectrum of morphologic components, with REAH having predominantly respiratory surface epithelium, seromucinous hamartomas having predominantly seromucinous glands, and CORE hamartomas having respiratory epithelium, seromucinous glands, bone, and cartilage. The etiology of these lesions is not fully understood. Another type of sinonasal hamartoma, chondromesenchymal hamartoma, is actually a neoplastic entity is driven by DICER1 mutations and is comprised of a range of immature to mature mesenchymal tissue and cartilage.

Answer: C. Squamous cell carcinoma ex-inverted papilloma

Histology: The lesion is composed of an endophytic proliferation of squamous epithelium beneath the surface of benign respiratory mucosa. Portions of this proliferation consist of rounded nests of admixed squamoid, transitional, and mucinous cells that lack significant cytologic atypia and have neutrophils transmigrating through the epithelium. However, other areas of the lesion show more complex, confluent, and irregular growth with markedly increased nuclear pleomorphism, nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio, conspicuous mitoses, and coarse chromatin with prominent nucleoli.

Discussion: The lesion in this case exhibits remnants of an inverted sinonasal papilloma with transformation to a squamous cell carcinoma, and the identification of both components is key to the diagnosis. Sinonasal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) can arise from several pathways, including conventional SCC, HPV-associated SCC, ex papilloma, and new translocation-driven entities such as DEK::AFF2 carcinoma. 5-10% of inverted papillomas can undergo malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma. The majority of inverted papillomas and associated squamous cell carcinomas harbor somatic EGFR mutations, with a subset driven by low-risk HPV. Despite conflicting reports in historical literature, recent evidence shows that high-risk HPV is not a common etiologic agent in inverted papillomas or carcinoma ex-papilloma.

Answer: A. HPV- associated ciliated adenosquamous carcinoma

Histology: The lesion is composed of nests to sheets of large, atypical cells with markedly pleomorphic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and scattered atypical mitoses that show a combination of pushing and infiltrative growth through background lymphocytes. There are scattered glandular spaces filled with cellular debris lined by atypical columnar cells, some of which are ciliated.

Discussion: HPV- associated squamous cell carcinoma generally has a non-keratinizing morphology, with tumor cells that have large nuclei, scant eosinophilic cytoplasm, and minimal keratinization. These carcinomas have several histologic variants, including keratinizing, basaloid, sarcomatoid, lymphoepithelial, and adenosquamous. The adenosquamous variant shows a mix of squamous and glandular morphologies that can rarely be ciliated, as can be seen in this case. Cilia formation can complicate differentiating the tumor from benign upper aerodigestive lesions but the ciliated cells are closely intermixed with the tumor cells and are positive for p16 and high-risk HPV RNA in-situ hybridization. In general, histologic variants of HPV-associated squamous cell carcinoma do not affect prognosis, which is more favorable than HPV-negative squamous cell carcinomas of the head and neck.

The College of American Pathologists guidelines recommend that all new squamous cell carcinomas arising in the oropharynx or neck metastasis of unknown primary should be tested for involvement by high-risk HPV via p16 immunohistochemistry. In squamous cell carcinoma of the oropharynx and levels II and III of the neck, p16 positivity is regarded as diagnostic of HPV positivity due to the high pretest probability for HPV involvement. Outside of these sites, however, HPV specific testing such as in-situ hybridization or PCR is required to confirm involvement by HPV due to the imperfect specificity for p16 in non-oropharyngeal sites.

Answer: D. Malakoplakia

Histology: The lesion is composed of syncytial sheets of histiocytes with foamy to granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and background chronic inflammation. Focal basophilic round to targetoid appearing cytoplasmic inclusions are scattered throughout.

Discussion: Malakoplakia is a rare, benign, mass-like lesion usually seen in the genitourinary tract and is associated with infection. It is composed of sheets of distinctive histocytes with eosinophilic granular cytoplasm called von Hansemann cells with interspersed acute and chronic inflammatory cells. The histiocytes also have basophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions called Michaelis-Gutmann bodies, which are a distinct diagnostic feature. These will stain positive for calcium. Malakoplakia of the bone is exceedingly rare, and some case reports have noted an association with osteomyelitis.

answer.text:
Answer: A. Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma

Histology: This lesion is composed of large cells with round, basophilic nuclei with focal nuclear molding and small nucleoli growing in a sheet-like to nested architecture with an infiltrative growth pattern, focal necrosis, and a high mitotic rate. The cytoplasm is not overwhelmingly abundant. On immunostains (not shown), the neoplastic cells were positive for chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and TTF-1.

Discussion: Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma is an aggressive, high grade carcinoid tumor comprised of large polygonal cells growing in an organoid pattern. The four types of neuroendocrine tumors of the lung are typical carcinoid tumor, atypical carcinoid tumor, large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, and small cell lung carcinoma. Typical and atypical carcinoid tumors are low grade lesions showing low amounts of proliferation (2 mitoses per 10 HPF for typical carcinoid, 2-10 per 10 HPF for atypical carcinoid) and mild nuclear atypia. Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma and small cell lung carcinoma are high grade lesions with significant proliferation (>11 mitoses per 10 HPF) and atypia and are composed of large and small cells, respectively. All of these lesions will have some neuroendocrine differentiation, but it may be lower in higher grade lesions. Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma and small cell lung carcinoma are also TTF-1 positive. In this case, the cells are not as large as expected and appear somewhat monotonous, lacking the vesicular chromatin usually present. Though it presents with a more typical carcinoid morphology, the mitotic rate and necrosis indicate a higher rate of proliferation, placing this lesion into the large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma category despite appearing closer to an atypical carcinoid.

Answer: B. Bronchiolitis obliterans

Histology: The lesion in this case has a patchy distribution involving the small bronchioles, with fibrosis and an inflammatory infiltrate completely or near-completely occluding the lumen of the bronchioles. Large bronchioles and the background emphysematous lung parenchyma are unaffected by this process.

Discussion: Bronchiolitis obliterans is a rare disease in which the bronchioles of the lung are narrowed or completely destroyed (obliterated). Proliferative bronchiolitis obliterans destroys the respiratory bronchioles by connective tissue initially forming a polypoid intraluminal lesion and progressively filling the lumen of the bronchiole. Constrictive bronchiolitis obliterans affects the larger bronchioles, which are destroyed by fibrosis. There is often a cellular chronic inflammatory infiltrate around the bronchioles. This is an irreversible process, and has a number of potential etiologies, including post infectious, autoimmune, transplant rejection/graft versus host disease, exposure to toxic fumes, and idiopathic.

Answer: A. Seminoma

Histology: The lesion is composed of nests of loosely cohesive cells with round to cuboidal nuclei, coarse chromatin, conspicuous nucleoli, and background chronic inflammation. The lesion is unencapsulated but relatively well circumscribed.

Discussion: Seminomas are the most common malignant germ cell tumor of the testis and most frequently occur in young adult males, but they do have a bimodal age distribution. The neoplastic cells are often accompanied by a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, as well as non-necrotizing granulomas. By immunohistochemistry, the neoplastic seminoma cells label for OCT 3/4, and are negative for hematolymphoid markers and cytokeratins. Like seminoma, diffuse large B cell lymphoma cells are also loosely cohesive, but they are negative for OCT 3/4 and instead label for CD45 (pan-lymphoid) and CD20 (B-cell lineage). Embryonal carcinoma, another type of malignant germ cell tumor, is histologically high-grade and labels for cytokeratins and CD30. Finally, spermatocytic tumors (formerly, spermatocytic seminomas) are composed of three different cell types (small, intermediate, and giant cells) and have a benign clinical course.

answer.text:
Answer: D. Angiosarcoma

Histology: The lesion is an infiltrative neoplasm composed of a vascular proliferation with anastomosing vessels, blood lakes, nuclear atypia and endothelial mitotic activity. Vascular spaces infiltrate irregularly through fat and around and through breast terminal duct lobular units.

Discussion: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular neoplasm. There are broadly to types of angiosarcoma in the breast: primary angiosarcoma and secondary (post-radiation) sarcoma. Primary angiosarcomas of the breast typically present as breast masses in pre-menopausal females, and the lesions are generally centered in the breast parenchyma. Secondary, or post-radiation, angiosarcomas of the breast typically present as skin changes in post-menopausal females approximately 7-10 years after breast radiation, and the lesions are generally centered in the dermis. Primary and secondary angiosarcomas of the breast may be widely infiltrative, and although the mainstay of treatment is complete surgical resection with widely clear margins, they frequently recur and cause significant morbidity and mortality.

The differential diagnosis of angiosarcoma includes benign vascular proliferations and other spindle cell lesions of the breast such as metaplastic carcinoma. Unlike atypical vascular lesions and hemangiomas, angiosarcomas display nuclear atypia, endothelial cell multilayering, mitotic activity, and infiltrative growth. Immunohistochemical stains can be used to classify spindle cell lesions of the breast. Angiosarcomas will label for markers used for endothelial differentiation, such as CD34, CD31, and ERG. Unlike breast carcinomas, angiosarcomas are typically negative for cytokeratins.

Answer: A. Traumatic Neuroma

Histology: The lesion consists of a disorganized proliferation of peripheral nerve bundles with intervening scar tissue. The nerve fibers form irregular clusters with intervening fibrous scar. The lesion is relatively well-circumscribed but not encapsulated, with surrounding skeletal muscle.

Discussion: Traumatic neuromas are non-neoplastic lesions that develop in the setting of previous trauma to an area, usually in the form of a prior biopsy or procedure at the site of the lesion. In contrast, a Schwannoma is a benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor composed entirely of Schwann cells, is encapsulated, has hyalinization of blood vessels, and has hypocellular (Antoni A) and hypercellular (Antoni B) areas. Neurofibromas are a benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor composed of all components of the nerve sheath, with spindled cells, hyalinized stroma, and mast cells.

Histology: The lesion is a generally well-defined nodule within the kidney with focal areas of infiltrative growth at the edge of the nodule. Answer: B. Squamous Cell Carcinoma

Histology: The lesion is composed of an invasive neoplasm composed of sheets and nests of cells with pleomorphic nuclei invading into the detrusor muscle. Nuclei have prominent, sometimes multiple nucleoli with focal nuclear molding and a high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio. There is also prominent lymphovascular invasion and focal necrosis. Of note, there are areas of benign urothelium overlying the invasive carcinoma.

Discussion: This lesion is a metastatic HPV-related squamous cell carcinoma from the cervix involving the bladder. Most primary squamous cell carcinomas of the bladder occur in the context of squamous metaplasia from a process causing chronic irritation, such as schistosomiasis. Primary squamous cell carcinoma is rare and more difficult to treat than urothelial carcinoma, as it is typically resistant to chemotherapy. Urothelial carcinoma can exhibit squamous features, which may be associated with a more aggressive and treatment resistant course. The basaloid appearance of the tumor, along with its location undermining benign urothelium, are suggestive of a carcinoma from another site that is involving the bladder as a metastasis or direct extension. In women, HPV-related basaloid squamous cell carcinoma is most commonly an extension from the gynecologic tract.

Histology: The lesion consists of an exophytic appearing squamous cell proliferation composed of papillary projections with fibrovascular cores. The squamous epithelium shows moderate nuclear atypia and koilocytic changes.

Discussion: Condyloma accuminata is an HPV-related sexually transmitted infection causing a wart-like lesion arising in the squamous mucosa of the genital area. The distal penile urethra, specifically the fossa navicularis, is lined by a non-keratinizing squamous epithelium, allowing the urethral meatus and distal urethra to be involved by these lesions. Lesions at this site are uncommon, and can be asymptomatic or cause symptoms of dysuria. HPV 6 and 11 commonly cause genital warts but do not commonly progress to HPV related neoplastic lesions like HPV 16 and 18. Immunostains for p16 will show diffuse, block like positivity. Unlike a carcinoma, the lesion is benign and will not have any features of invasion.

Answer: C. Clear cell hidradenoma

Histologic Description: This is a somewhat cystic lesion with solid and papillary architectures. The neoplastic cells closely resemble urothelium in that they have a transitional type appearance and are associated with flatted cells at the top which resemble urothelial umbrella cells. The stroma is hyalinized, and there is essentially no mitotic activity. These features are typical of clear cell hidradenoma, an adnexal neoplasm.

Differential Diagnosis: Metastatic urothelial carcinoma would have a similar pattern but would demonstrate greater cytologic atypia and mitotic activity. This would be extremely unusual in the absence of a history of urothelial carcinoma. Given the patient"s history of prostatic adenocarcinoma, a metastases from that tumor is a significant concern; however, the absence of immunoreactivity for prostatic markers like NKX3.1, as well as diffuse immunoreactivity for GATA3, excluded that possibility. Invasive squamous cell carcinoma would demonstrate keratinization as well as greater cytologic atypia and mitotic activity.

Recently, clear cell hidradenomas have been shown to have the same gene fusion has been identified in mucoepidermoid carcinoma of salivary glands (CRTC1/3-MAML2).

Answer: B. Xp11 translocation carcinoma

Histologic Description: This is a clear cell neoplasm with a solid/nested architecture. The stroma is somewhat hyalinized, and there are associated psammoma bodies. In many areas, there are prominent subnuclear vacuoles. The neoplasm is essentially non-immunoreactive for carbonic anhydrase 9 (CA-IX) and cytokeratin 7, but demonstrates strong nuclear immunoreactivity for TFE3. This supports the diagnosis of Xp11 translocation renal cell carcinoma.

Differential Diagnosis: Many areas of the neoplasm overlaps with clear cell carcinoma. One difference is that the stroma of clear cell RCC is typically more cellular and hypervascular than the hyalinized stroma of an Xp11 translocation RCC. The absence of CA-IX labeling and strong TFE3 labeling excludes clear cell RCC. TCEB1 mutated renal cell carcinomas also have extensive clear cells, and can overlap in areas with clear cell RCC. However, TCEB1-mutated RCCs typically have prominent smooth muscle stroma and branching arborizing papillary architecture. Clear cell papillary renal cell carcinoma atypically demonstrates subnuclear vacuoles, and may have a prominent tubular architecture. However, clear cell papillary RCC labels for both cytokeratin 7 and carbonic anhydrase 9, but not for TFE3.

This case illustrated the ability of Xp11 translocation RCC to demonstrate subnuclear vacuoles that mimic those of clear cell papillary RCC.

answer.text:
Answer: C. Malignant phyllodes tumor

Histologic Description: The vast majority of this neoplasm consists of a nondescript high grade pleomorphic spindle cell sarcoma. The neoplastic cells demonstrate high mitotic activity including atypical mitoses, and extensive necrosis. Focally, after multiple additional sections were taken, a lower grade phyllodes tumor component with liposarcomatous differentiation was identified. This latter area was key to the diagnosis of malignant phyllodes tumor in this case, as the high grade spindle cell areas demonstrated no specific immunostaining.

Differential Diagnosis: Metaplastic carcinoma would be expected to either demonstrate immunoreactivity for epithelial markers and or a carcinomatous component. A primary mammary sarcoma is a diagnosis of exclusion, since phyllodes tumors with stromal overgrowth overlap with primary mammary sarcomas. Fibromatosis would lack the pleomorphism, mitotic activity and necrosis of the current case.

This case highlights the utility of additional tissue sampling in characterizing high grade pleomorphic neoplasms. Multiple rounds of immunostains on a high grade anaplastic component are less useful than well taken additional sections.
